title: Key Republican says he will vote for Todd Blanche to become attorney general after other senators defect – live
summary: Senator Bill Cassidy, who will not be returning to Congress after losing his Louisiana primary to a Trump-backed candidate, said he would support the AG nominee
body: Donald Trump announced a list of deals and investments that aim to bolster mining, totaling more than $2 billion in projects and mining school investments. The largest chunk will go to the California-based company Sila Nanotechnologies to build a battery facility and expand production, coming as a $1.4b investment from the defense department. The department will also give $400m to Sunrise Energy Metals to develop scandium, which is used in fighter jets and spacecraft, among other companies. The Export-Import Bank, which provides financing to support US exports, is also investing in a boron deposit, battery manufacturing, and tantalum and niobium to make electronics, magnet, and steel. Donald Trump once again targeted Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, this time writing a post on Truth Social saying she should “re-visit her hastily made decision” after she dismissed vandalism charges against Olympic canoeist David Hearn last week. Trump reposted images from a photographer of what seemed like the reflecting pool showing “slashes”, according to the US president, who also claimed “there were witnesses to the VANDALISM.” “U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro should re-visit her hastily made decision,” he wrote. These comments are just the latest in a series of snubs against Pirro, a longtime Trump ally. After her decision to dismiss the charges, the president accused her of having “folded like an umbrella.” He also told NBC News that he didn’t “understand why she did such a stupid thing.” Officers for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will be equipped with much-delayed body cameras by the end of next month, it was reported on Friday. But experts have questioned the transparency of a policy that allows the ICE director to restrict the public release of footage unless “it is in the best interests of the agency”. Pressure has mounted on the Trump administration to provide body cameras after people caught up in encounters with federal immigration personnel suffered death or serious injuries. Two men were shot and killed by ICE agents, in Texas and Maine, last month in circumstances similar to the death of another man during a traffic stop in Illinois last September. None of the officers involved was wearing a camera. Tom Homan, Trump’s so-called border czar, said last month that ICE officers would be required to have at least one body camera recording during future vehicle stops. Policy for body-worn cameras was first established in a February 2025 ICE directive, but funding for their provision was held up by this year’s partial government shutdown, Homan said. Louisiana congressional candidate Blake Miguez, a Republican state senator who was the subject of a police report accusing him of a rape that he denies, waited until the final day of a three-day qualifying period to make clear his intentions for the upcoming midterm elections. Miguez on Friday afternoon signed up to run in Louisiana’s sixth congressional district – despite knowing, if he did so, he would have to again compete for a coveted Donald Trump endorsement which he had previously secured while campaigning for another US House seat. Miguez had first signed up to run for Louisiana’s fifth US House district seat for a primary initially scheduled for May, and he had won the president’s endorsement. But that race was postponed until the November midterms after the US supreme court’s landmark voting rights decision in Callais v Louisiana prompted the state to redraw the boundaries of its congressional districts. Those redrawn boundaries pushed a residence that Miguez bought in March in the state capital of Baton Rouge from the fifth district to the sixth, as the Louisiana Illuminator news outlet reported. In late July, after his campaign website had temporarily become blank and password protected, a spokesperson for Miguez acknowledged to the Guardian that the state senator was left hoping to again “earn” Trump’s endorsement as he weighed announcing a run for office “under the new district lines”. Politico, citing sources with direct knowledge of the matter, reported a day later that Miguez was mulling a run in the new sixth district. The outlet furthermore reported that Trump officials had told Miguez privately that he would not have the president’s endorsement — at least not immediately — if he opted for a sixth district run. In safely Republican districts like the sixth in Louisiana, Trump’s endorsement is eagerly sought by candidates from the party he has led across two presidencies. Another Republican candidate who has also formally signed up to run in Louisiana’s sixth district has already expressed his confidence that Miguez won’t have Trump’s endorsement. “What I do know is he’s not getting the president’s endorsement in the sixth district,” Louisiana state senator Rick Edmonds said to reporters after signing up to run there on Wednesday. Miguez’s website was reactivated on Friday. It had replaced a prior mention of his Trump endorsement with a pledge to work alongside the president if eventually elected. He also didn’t mention having Trump’s endorsement in a social media post announcing his signing up to run in the sixth district, saying he qualified there because that area had “given so much” to him through the years. An additional complication with which Miguez has had to grapple is a 2007 police report containing a rape allegation made against him by an ex-girlfriend. He denies the claim, and it never led to formal charges. But that document’s existence first became public when the Atlantic and the Guardian each published separate stories on 11 March, after Miguez had locked down Trump’s fifth district endorsement. The Atlantic also wrote that the police report raised concerns within the president’s team that Miguez “either wasn’t fully vetted or wasn’t forthcoming about discoverable documents from his past” while he successfully pursued Trump’s endorsement. Miguez’s opponents are bound to invoke that police report ahead of a 3 November open primary – and a 12 December runoff if necessary. In fact, his qualification on Friday was immediately met with a mass text from a federal political action committee calling itself End Predator Abuse that provided recipients a link to a website with the police report. “Blake Miguez CANNOT be our congressman,” the group’s text read. In the months since the disclosure of that police report, US House members Eric Swalwell and Tony Gonzales – a California Democrat and a Texas Republican, respectively – heeded bipartisan calls to resign over allegations of sexual misconduct against both. Then, on 10 July, Democratic US Senate hopeful Graham Platner of Maine withdrew his candidacy after detailed sexual assault allegations were made against him. And Republican congressman Max Miller of Ohio has been met with growing calls to resign over domestic abuse allegations. By an overwhelming majority, the Senate just advanced legislation that would extend government funding through 11 December – after the midterm elections. Current spending expires on 30 September. As a reminder, before the House went on recess last month, lawmakers approved a stopgap measure to head off a government shutdown until 4 December, sending it to the upper chamber for consideration. Top congressional Republicans have argued that an extension to the continuing resolution is necessary to ensure that Democrats do not block government funding measures in the Senate. They did so last year for a record 43 days in protest against the expiration of tax credits that lowered some healthcare costs, and twice again this year, to push for reforms to immigration enforcement operations after the killings of two US citizens in Minneapolis. Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the banking committee, has slammed reports that Donald Trump is attempting to fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook again, despite an earlier supreme court ruling this year that protects her from dismissal while she fights the Trump administration’s allegations that she has committed mortgage fraud. Warren said that the president “is tanking the economy, and he is desperate to shift the blame for higher costs and higher interest rates. So he’s once again trying to illegally take over America’s central bank.” She added: “If he [Trump] is successful, it will be working families who pay the price. We will fight back to make sure he fails.” Donald Trump has started his state department roundtable on American mining, we’ll bring you the latest lines as it gets under way. A number of Donald Trump’s other nominations were also confirmed in the Senate today. By a vote of 51-47 along party lines, the upper chamber’s confirmations included David Cummins to lead the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), and the new Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) administrator, Cameron Hamilton. Senator Bill Cassidy, the last Republican who was undecided about Todd Blanche’s nomination as attorney general, said he would vote to confirm Donald Trump’s pick to lead the justice department. His “yes” vote, will now likely clear the way for Blanche to receive the 50 votes needed, effectively saving his nomination. This comes after Senator Lisa Murkowski, a moderate Republican from Alaska, said earlier that she would oppose Blanche’s nomination. “The politicization – even weaponization – of the Department did not start with this administration but has accelerated during it,” she said in a statement, adding that she does not have confidence that Blanche would be able to “check the worst impulses of this administration”. A US federal appeals court has ordered the Trump administration to halt construction of the US president’s $400m White House ballroom, in a fresh blow to the controversial project. title: US police officer accused of killing three people in Mexico arrested at border
summary: Chad Eberle of Texas charged over deadly shooting in Saltillo that officials say stemmed from custody dispute
body: A Texas police officer has been arrested in Mexico after authorities there accused him of killing three people and critically injuring the mother of his child in what investigators say stemmed from a dispute over the custody of the minor. The Coahuila attorney general’s office said 35-year-old Chad Eberle was arrested on Wednesday at the border on a warrant accusing him of femicide and qualified homicide, according to La Razon de Mexico, a newspaper based in Mexico City. Under Mexican law, femicide refers to the intentional killing of a woman or girl because of her gender. According to La Razon, the deadly shooting happened in July in Saltillo, Mexico, after an argument over Eberle allegedly not having permission to take his three-year-old son. Two women and one man were killed in the attack. The victims were identified by La Razon with the first names and ages of Ana Laura, 44; Laura Jaquelín, 22; and Emanuel, 44. The child’s 26-year-old mother was also shot in the head and remained in critical condition, officials said. Investigators said Eberle was arrested while attempting to cross from Mexico into Texas through the international bridge at Piedras Negras, across from Eagle Pass, KTXS reported. Eberle had left the residence with his son in a gray Chevrolet Silverado, prompting investigators to launch a manhunt as they tracked the vehicle toward the Texas border, the US Sun reported. He was then intercepted before he could re-enter the US with the child. The three-year-old was unharmed and was later placed in the care of Coahuila’s child welfare agency. The San Antonio Express identified Eberle as a police officer in the central Texas town of Santa Anna. Before that, he worked as a deputy constable with Bexar county – which includes San Antonio – and also served as a police officer for the Northside independent school district. The Express reported that Eberle also held law enforcement positions in the Texas communities of Somerset, Marble Falls, Gregory, near Corpus Christi, Lockney in the state’s panhandle, and Bangs in the west. According to the newspaper, a 2022 Facebook post from the Lockney police department described Eberle as an army veteran. In a social media post on Thursday, Coahuila attorney general Federico Fernández said: “It is reported that at [9.59p] Chad ‘N’ has been admitted to the Saltillo men’s penitentiary in compliance with [an] arrest warrant, where he has been placed at the disposal of the competent judicial authority, in accordance with the corresponding procedure.” He added: “Likewise, the minor is already in the city of Saltillo, under the custody and care of the prosecutor’s office for boys, girls and the family (Pronnif), in order to guarantee the comprehensive protection of his rights.” Texas news outlet Coleman Today obtained a statement from Santa Anna city officials which described Eberle as “one of our reserve officers … [who] was on a personal leave of absence until December. “The Santa Anna police department has been in contact with the US consulate in Mexico and [the Texas commission on law enforcement].” That statement also said Eberle was “an unpaid reserve police officer hired in November 2025 and worked one weekend per month. “Due to the ongoing investigation, no other public comment will be made.”

title: US Senate passes Russia sanctions bill championed by Lindsey Graham
summary: Late senator spent final days of his life working to advance bill that will now head to the House after 86-11 Senate vote
body: By a large, bipartisan margin, the US Senate on Friday approved a bill intended to punish Russia and countries that buy its petroleum exports over the invasion of Ukraine, capping a legislative push that was spurred by the death of its champion, the Republican senator Lindsey Graham. The measure, renamed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act in honor of the late senator’s work on the issue, was approved by an 86-11 vote. Rand Paul of Kentucky was the sole Republican to oppose the legislation, together with 10 Democrats. The bill would impose new sanctions and visa bans on Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and top military commanders, as well as put tariffs of up to 500% on the country’s exports. It would also allow Donald Trump to impose levies of up to 100% on goods from countries that are the top five importers of Russian oil and gas. The proposal was a top priority for Graham, a Republican senator from South Carolina who spent the final days of his life working to advance it. But the effort had became mired in months of negotiations between the White House and Senate leadership. After Graham’s sudden death last month at the age of 71 following a trip to Kyiv, party leaders announced an agreement to get the bill through the chamber and honor his legacy as an ally of Ukraine. The Senate took the first step toward advancing it last month, on the day of Graham’s funeral, with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, watching from the chamber. “This bill forces those primary countries keeping Russia’s economy afloat to make a simple yet critical choice – a choice between doing business with America or buying cheap Russian energy,” said Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to his seat after his death. Graham, who presided over the Senate and announced the bill’s passage, added: “This legislation tells Russia’s customers that the United States of America will not sit by while they fund Putin’s assault.” The measure was a relatively rare bipartisan accomplishment ahead of November’s midterm elections, where Democrats hope to channel voter sentiment against Trump to regain control of Congress. “By imposing steep sanctions that will further drain the Kremlin’s war chest, Congress is delivering an important reminder to Putin and his allies that this is a losing war and authoritarianism will never go unchallenged,” said Chuck Schumer, the minority leader. “I urge Trump to use these sanctions to hit Putin where it hurts. Continuing to appease Putin won’t work.” After the vote, Zelenskyy thanked the US Senate, writing on X that the bill’s advancement “certainly helps increase pressure ⁠on the aggressor to bring this insane Russian war against our ‌independence and our people to an end”. Ursula ⁠von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, also cheered the Senate’s action. “Together, let us drain Russia’s means to continue a war it cannot win,” she wrote on X. “With hard-hitting, complementary ⁠sanctions, Europe and the United States can once again show what historic partners can ‌achieve when we act together.” The measure now heads to the House of Representatives, which may consider once it returns from recess at the end of August. Some Democrats have warned that the bill would give Trump new tariff powers at a time when he has put such levies at the center of his trade policy. Paul and Democratic senator Ron Wyden had offered an amendment that would have stripped some of the new tariff authority from the text, but the Senate rejected it by a 32-64 vote. “This bill gives him so much discretion that Trump can ultimately decide what countries to tariff, or what countries to exempt. And he can modify tariffs at his will,” said Wyden, who voted against the bill. “Trump can pick and choose even more countries to tariff every 180 days, but there is no mechanism in this bill for Congress to roll back these tariffs,” he continued. “If Congress passes this bill, members will be condoning the tariff chaos of the last year and a half – and inviting more.” Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, and Don Beyer, the senior Democrat on the joint economic committee, criticized the legislation for creating “sweeping new tariff authorities that the president could weaponize with abandon, as he has repeatedly done in the past”. Noting that Trump just weeks ago imposed new 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods, the two Democrats said: “We welcome our Senate colleagues’ urgent effort to support Ukraine and punish Russia for its continued illegal war, but this bill would not achieve those goals. Instead, it would allow President Trump to dodge holding Russia accountable and impose yet more tariffs in his destructive trade wars, leaving Americans to foot the bill.”

title: At least one person dead in California wildfire allegedly sparked by chainsaw
summary: Police arrested Herbert Wayne Smith, 65, in connection with the Gann fire, which has burned more than 15 sq miles in Calaveras county
body: At least one person has died in a wildfire burning in the foothills of California’s Sierra Nevada mountain range that officials believed was sparked by a man using a chainsaw. Police arrested Herbert Wayne Smith, 65, in connection with the Gann fire, which has destroyed seven buildings, scorched more than 15 sq miles in Calaveras county and killed a well-known dog breeder in the town of Angels Camp. In an interview with KCRA, Smith told reporters he did not mean to spark the fire. Monday was his birthday, he said, and he had been using machinery to cut scraps in order collect money for a celebratory meal with his wife. “I’m so sorry for everything that’s happened,” Smith told the news station. “This is going to destroy my life, one way or another.” Officials allege that Smith is responsible for “recklessly causing” the blaze on Monday while “operating equipment capable of producing sparks” without clearing flammable vegetation as required, according to the California department of forestry and fire protection. Prosecutors will determine whether to file criminal charges. In 2018, Smith was charged with igniting another fire, KCRA reported, and was accused of “willfully and unlawfully [setting] fire to any forest, brush, or other flammable material which is on any land that is not his own, or under his legal control, without the permission of the owner, lessee, or agent of the owner or lessee of the land”. He pleaded no contest and received a sentence of 36 months’ probation. As of Friday morning, the Gann fire had burned more than 10,000 acres and was about 40% contained. Investigators will determine whether the fire contributed to the death of the person found in a burned home near the town of Angels Camp, the Calaveras county sheriff’s office said. Friends have identified the victim as Susan Solari and a neighbor told CBS Sacramento that she refused to leave her dogs. “I told them she was there, that her dogs were there and she couldn’t get her dogs out,” Joan Wilson told the outlet. “She wasn’t going to leave them.” The Gann fire comes amid a grueling fire season in the American west. Three major fires have continued to burn around the city of Spokane in north-eastern Washington and have destroyed at least 800 buildings. A 37-year-old man has been arrested for allegedly sparking one of the fires, and court documents accuse him of studying how to maximize the blaze’s destruction. No deaths have been reported in Washington. Officials reported on Thursday that cooler temperatures and calmer winds have allowed firefighters to make progress. Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Trump renews bid to fire Fed governor Lisa Cook despite supreme court ruling
summary: White House continues to target Cook despite decision from justices that upheld Federal Reserve’s independence
body: Donald Trump is attempting once again to oust the US Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook over allegations of mortgage fraud, despite a recent US supreme court decision that upheld the central bank’s independence. Cook reportedly received a letter from the White House this week that provided notice, in accordance to the supreme court’s June ruling, that Trump was “considering removing” her from her Fed position over the same claims of mortgage fraud that he levied against her last summer. The letter, first reported by ABC News, accused Cook of falling “well short of the standard” required of a sitting Fed governor and requested she provide a written response to the allegations within three weeks. The supreme court in June ruled 5-4 that Cook was entitled to stay on as Fed governor while she fights the president’s allegations, writing in its majority opinion that Trump “failed to afford Cook the procedural protections to which she was entitled by statute”. “Without such protections, she could not properly dispute the charges the president laid against her,” the justices said. In response to the White House’s letter, one of Cook’s lawyers, Abbe D Lowell, called the allegations “as baseless now as they were a year ago when President Trump tried to remove Governor Cook and interfere with the independence of the Federal Reserve”. “No matter what President Trump tries to do next, this much is clear under the facts and Supreme Court precedent – there is no valid cause for removing Governor Cook,” Lowell said in a statement. “As we did before, we will challenge this latest pretext and preserve her position and the historic role of the Fed.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Cook was appointed by Joe Biden in 2022 to a 14-year term that will end in 2038. She is the first Black woman to serve as a Fed governor. Before she joined the Fed, she served on Barack Obama’s council of economic advisers and has taught at Harvard University and Stanford University. Trump first abruptly fired Cook last August in an unprecedented attack on the central bank’s independence. The White House accused her of wrongly designating two separate properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residence and failing to report rental income on her Atlanta property for two years. Cook denied the allegations and sued the Trump administration for firing her without cause or proper procedure. Cook and her legal team have maintained that the claims of mortgage fraud are based on “inadvertent” paperwork errors and that the administration is “cherrypicking” facts. Cook’s firing and ongoing legal battles also coincided with Trump’s attacks on the Fed for not lowering rates. Cook, along with then Fed chair, Jerome Powell, had backed the central bank’s decision not to lower rates, which drew the ire of the White House. Trump called Powell “too stupid and too political” and launched a justice department investigation into his renovations of the Fed’s headquarters in Washington, which has since been dropped. The Fed is now under the leadership of Kevin Warsh, a Trump pick who had previously shown favor towards cutting rates. Warsh has maintained that he will make decisions based on economic data, not the will of the president, and has made it his mission to fight the country’s heightened inflation, which typically is addressed by rate hikes. “We’re an independent central bank,” he said in response to questioning from Democratic House members at a hearing in July. “We’re honored to be independent.”

title: Argentina’s government posts ICE-style video of immigration operation
summary: Social media video shows 60-year-old woman being led away in handcuffs, but she was released minutes later
body: The Argentinian government posted a video on social media showing a 60-year-old woman being led away in handcuffs by two federal police officers during an immigration operation in Buenos Aires. The woman’s face is shown unblurred in the video, which has nearly 1m views and depicts one of hundreds of such operations carried out by the administration of the far-right president, Javier Milei, directly inspired by Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown in the US. Visibly distressed, appearing to be in pain and with one hand bandaged, the woman is shown against a heavy metal soundtrack as the words “Illegal foreigner or criminal record? Out!” flash across the screen. In another video, she is described as “a Peruvian national subject to an arrest warrant for fraud and robbery”. But there was no arrest warrant for her. The woman, who asked to be identified only by her initials, PLS, said she was released just minutes after being paraded in handcuffs before photographers and television crews covering the operation, which took place last February. “They just drove me around the block and said: ‘Get out. You’re free.’ I asked: ‘Why did you put me through all this?’” she said. “My face was everywhere on social media. I started getting calls from relatives living abroad – back in Peru, in Spain, the US and Germany – asking me: ‘What happened? What did you do?’” she added. According to her lawyer, PLS is a legal permanent resident and was subject only to a “whereabouts inquiry” – requiring her to be notified about a separate case – which, under Argentinian law, does not entail arrest or any other form of coercion. “Her detention was unlawful, and the authorities used it as propaganda for their operations against immigrants,” said Lucía Galoppo, a lawyer at the NGO Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS), which is representing PLS. CELS sees her case as a striking example of how Milei is reshaping the country’s immigration laws to bring them closer to those of Trump – whom the Argentinian president openly admires – including by creating an Argentinian version of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Checks on people’s immigration status existed before, but they have become far more frequent, large-scale operations involving not only immigration agents but federal police. Much like Trump, Milei has turned raids in poorer, traditionally immigrant neighbourhoods into a “public spectacle”, said Galoppo. Since taking office in December 2023, the self-styled libertarian has introduced a series of changes to immigration law by decree, bypassing congress. The latest came in late July, when Milei invoked his claim that there had been an “anti-Argentina” wave since the World Cup to justify a decree allowing the deportation of foreigners who promote “messages of hate” against the country or any Argentinian citizen. Critics pointed to the irony that, had countries Milei recently visited adopted the same rule, the president himself could have been expelled after insulting Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez. Other decrees include ending the automatic right to permanent residency for foreigners who have a child born in the country or marry an Argentinian citizen, and requiring immigrants to prove they have sufficient financial means to support themselves – in a country where more than 40% of workers are informally employed. While making it harder to obtain documentation, Milei has also restricted free access to public hospitals, previously available to everyone but now limited to permanent residents, except in emergencies. “The state is manufacturing a problem to manufacture a security-based response,” said Galoppo. “Argentina doesn’t have an immigration problem,” she added. In the 2022 census, immigrants made up 4.2%, the lowest proportion since records began in 1869. Galoppo believes Milei is targeting immigrants as part of a strategy to create an “internal enemy” that distracts from domestic problems – alongside corruption scandals, his “chainsaw” austerity policies have brought inflation under control, but unemployment and poverty have risen. Milei did not respond to requests for comment. CELS filed freedom of information requests with the government about its immigration operations. There were 851 between 1 January and 26 June. The government provided further details on only 590 of them, in which just 2.2% of the foreigners stopped were found to have irregular immigration status. “These operations are highly theatrical, deploying hundreds of police officers in an attempt to imitate raids in the US, but the tiny number of people found to have irregular status shows they are not justified,” said Galoppo. In the lawsuit filed against the state on behalf of PLS, CELS alleges that she was subjected to unlawful deprivation of liberty, degrading treatment, public humiliation and abuse of authority. PLS has lived in Argentina since 2006. The “whereabouts inquiry” involving her relates to a 2021 case. In it, a person whose phone was stolen alleged that money had been transferred from their account to one in PLS’s name and then to a third account. PLS denies any involvement, saying her own phone had been stolen months earlier and may have been used to create an account in her name. Her lawyer said being sought for notification did not justify her detention. The security ministry also did not respond to requests for comment. PLS said she felt ashamed and afraid to leave home after the operation, costing her her livelihood as a street food vendor. “If I saw a police officer, I was frightened thinking they might arrest me,” she said. But she added that she had no intention of leaving: “I’ve done nothing wrong. I’m not a criminal. I’m someone who works. I liked Argentina, and I want to stay here.”

title: US woman who killed husband two decades ago admits murder of firefighter wife
summary: Yolanda Olejniczak Marodi pleads guilty to killing Rebecca Marodi, decorated fire captain who fought Eaton blaze
body: A California woman this week admitted to killing her wife, a decorated fire captain who fought the deadly 2025 Los Angeles wildfires, by stabbing her – the same fate she previously delivered to her husband and had served a decade in prison for. Yolanda Olejniczak Marodi, 54, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to second-degree murder after killing her wife, Rebecca “Becky” Marodi, 49, a California fire captain, at their home in February 2025, just a month after Becky, as she was known, battled the Eaton blaze that killed 19. Rebecca Marodi, who was assigned to the French Valley Cal Fire station in Riverside county was found with multiple stab wounds to her neck, chest and back at the couple’s home in Ramona, near San Diego. She had said she wanted to end the marriage. A warrant for Olejniczak Marodi’s arrest was issued days later. Detectives said home security footage had shown Rebecca Marodi running from her wife of two years, screaming: “Yolanda! Please! I don’t want to die!” According to investigators, Olejniczak Marodi, who was seen holding a knife and with blood on her arms in the surveillance film, replied: “You should have thought of that before.” Olejniczak Marodi was captured on video loading “pets, random items and some luggage” and loading them into an SUV, according to the warrant seen at the time by ABC News. About 75 minutes after the attack, records from homeland security showed Olejniczak Marodi crossing the nearby border into Mexico. Investigators later found that the then suspect messaged a friend: “Rebecca came home and told me she was leaving me. We had a big fight, and I hurt her. I’m sorry.” It emerged that Olejniczak Marodi had been in prison from 2004 to 2013 after being convicted of voluntary manslaughter in the 2000 stabbing death of her then husband Jim Olejniczak. He, too, had recently informed her he was ending the marriage. After she fled this time, Mexican law enforcement officers arrested her at a hotel in Mexicali in March 2025 and she was later handed over to US marshals in San Diego and booked on suspicion of murder. She initially pleaded not guilty. Andrea Winter, a friend of Rebecca, told the Los Angeles Times that Olejniczak Marodi was jealous of her wife’s popularity and exhibited “controlling, isolating behavior” before the killing. Winter said Rebecca had not disclosed that her wife had been convicted of stabbing her previous husband to death. “Yolanda was very insecure,” Winter told the outlet. “Becky has this magnetic personality and everybody liked her. I think Yolanda was very jealous of that and that Becky was this bright light.” She added: “Becky was a kind person and paid the absolute price for that by trusting the wrong person.” Olejniczak Marodi is scheduled to be sentenced on 2 September and faces 36 years to life in a state prison.

title: Judge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protections
summary: Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians
body: Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections. On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US. Saris’s decision follows a 6-3 supreme court ruling in June allowing the Trump administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians of TPS, which granted them permission to work and live legally in the US. The supreme court’s conservative majority overturned lower court rulings in New York and Washington DC, which had blocked the administration from ending TPS for more than 350,000 Haitians and about 6,100 Syrians. A TPS designation allows eligible people from certain countries facing crises including civil war and environmental disasters to remain in the US temporarily, protects them from deportation and allows them to work legally. In her 15-page ruling, Saris wrote that “as a logical matter, plaintiffs’ arguments rest upon a self-contradictory, self-defeating foundation”. According to Saris, the plaintiffs’ argument undermined itself, because if the homeland security department (DHS) lacked the authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation, it also would have lacked the authority to issue the designation initially. “South Sudan’s original TPS designation would thus be invalid by the same token as its termination,” Saris wrote. In response to the ruling, James Percival, a DHS general counsel said on X: “Every other TPS judge must do the same! Every day these ‘administrative stays’ are in effect is a day the American people are denied what they voted for.” The Guardian has contacted African Communities Together for comment. The Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants comes despite the US government’s own highest-level travel warnings for Americans to several countries affected, including South Sudan, Haiti and Syria. In the case of South Sudan, the country has been ravaged by years of civil war and political instability that have displaced millions. Since gaining independence in 2011, more than 400,000 people have been killed in conflict, with fighting and ethnic violence continuing to claim civilian lives. The DHS moved in November to terminate TPS for South Sudan, saying the country ‌no longer met the conditions for the designation, which was first issued in 2011. The department’s action would have led to the end of protections for more than 232 South Sudanese and at least 73 South Sudanese with pending applications. An earlier order by Saris had blocked that from happening. After the supreme court’s ruling, lawyers for a group of South Sudanese nationals and the non-profit African Communities Together urged Saris to once again block the ‌end of TPS on new grounds that the justices had not addressed. That included an argument that the DHS lacked authority to terminate TPS because the statute that created the TPS program in 1990 referred only to the attorney general as the official who had authority to extend and terminate the deportation protections. The DHS was established later, in 2002, after the September 11 attacks. Most of the justice department’s immigration-related functions were transferred to it at that time. Saris, who was appointed by Bill Clinton, concluded Congress had likewise transferred authority over TPS to the DHS. Since 2001, TPS holders have paid $7.8bn annually in taxes and contributed $262bn to the US economy, according to the advocacy organization Fwd.us. Many TPS holders are employed in critical industries already facing worker shortages across the country, including construction, hospitality and healthcare. Losing TPS can leave immigrants without legal status vulnerable to arrest, detention, and deportation, even with pending asylum or green card applications. Some may face immigration court proceedings with limited options to stay in the US. Those ordered removed could be deported and barred from returning for years. Reuters contributed reporting

title: Appeals court halts construction of Trump’s $400m White House ballroom
summary: Ruling put on hold for two weeks, allowing administration to appeal to US supreme court
body: A US federal appeals court has ordered the Trump administration to halt construction of the US president’s $400m White House ballroom, in a fresh blow to the controversial project. Donald Trump, who demolished the historic East Wing of the White House last year to make way for planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people. But in a major setback in a case testing ⁠his presidential authority, the Washington-based US ⁠court of appeals for the District of Columbia circuit upheld a preliminary injunction in a divided 2-1 order on Friday. The appeals court put ⁠its ruling on hold for two weeks, allowing the administration to appeal to the US supreme court. Writing on social media, Trump described the ruling as “totally wrong” and said an appeal would be filed. Explaining their majority decision, Judges Patricia Millet and Bradley Garcia wrote: “Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence.” The judges also said it was for US Congress to determine whether the ballroom could ultimately be built. “Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help,” they wrote. “This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy,” the judges added. “This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom. “What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the constitution and laws require.” Trump criticized the decision, which he argued “severely jeopardizes the lives and welfare of the people who work, and will be working”, at the White House. “This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety.” A third judge on the panel, Neomi Rao, who was appointed by Trump, dissented and sided with the president’s assertion that the ballroom project was within his authority. Her position earned praised from the president in his social media statement on Friday. The injunction was won by the National Trust for Historic ⁠Preservation, which sued last year after the Trump administration tore down the East Wing and began building a 90,000 sq ft (8,360 sq meter) ballroom without seeking authorization from Congress. The latest decision supports an earlier ruling issued by a US federal judge in April, which limited the construction project only to the undergound part of the project deemed necessary on national security grounds while blocking the hospitality facility envisioned by Trump for entertaining guests. At the time, Trump lambasted that decision, by Judge Richard Leon – appointed to the bench during George W Bush’s presidency – as the work of a “Trump Hating” judge who he alleged had “gone out of his way to undermine National Security, and to make sure that this Great Gift to America gets delayed, or doesn’t get built”.

title: Businessman was ‘preparing champagne’ to celebrate Caruana Galizia murder, court hears
summary: Taxi driver says he acted as middleman between Yorgen Fenech and three men already convicted of €150,000 contract killing
body: The businessman accused of paying for hitmen to murder the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was impatient for the killing to take place, and once texted from his boat to say he was “preparing champagne” to celebrate, a jury in Malta has heard. Yorgen Fenech, the 44-year-old heir to a property empire that includes several Hilton hotels, is on trial in Malta for complicity in the murder of Caruana Galizia. She died in a car bombing in October 2017 after publishing a series of revelations about senior politicians that were so damaging they triggered a snap general election. The key witness in the case, a taxi driver who says he acted as middleman between Fenech and three men already convicted of accepting €150,000 (£128,000) to carry out the killing, took the stand on Friday to begin his testimony. Melvin Theuma, who has been living under witness protection since agreeing to testify in return for a pardon, said Fenech had told him to contact a known criminal and set up the killing because he wanted to protect his uncle Raymond Fenech, the head of the family business. “Bring him here, I need him to kill Daphne because she’s going to publish information about Uncle Ray,” Theuma claimed Fenech had told him. Theuma has previously testified that over time the explanation changed, and the hit was designed to stop revelations about Yorgen himself. The conversation took place in April 2017. The two men were friends, having known each other for years, although Theuma told the jury it was not an equal relationship. “He’s a lion and I’m a mosquito,” Theuma said of the accused. The taxi driver, who had cultivated a friendship with Fenech over a shared interest in horseracing and betting, is regarded by the prosecution as key to securing a conviction. He has given police multiple recordings of conversations he had with Fenech after the murder. Before taking the stand, Theuma had to be certified as fit to give evidence, having previously tried to take his own life. In 2020, having already secured a pardon, he swallowed acid and slit his own throat. He will be allowed to give evidence seated, with his back to Fenech and his lawyers, having previously complained of intimidation. He began his testimony by apologising to the victim’s family, saying: “My cross was too much to bear; I can’t imagine what theirs was like.” After receiving the order from Fenech, Theuma said he went to the docks in Marsa, where the hitmen, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio and their associate Vincent Muscat, used a warehouse known as the potato shed as a base. “Alfred got into my taxi and I told him ‘I have someone who wants to kill Daphne Caruana Galizia’. “He asked if the person could pay, and I said yes, of course.” Theuma said he never told the hitmen who had sent him. He told the court Fenech had agreed to the price, but then asked him to call off the attack after Malta’s then prime minister, Joseph Muscat, called a snap general election. Instead, he asked Theuma to place a €150,000 bet for him on Muscat securing a second term. When Muscat was returned to power with a landslide victory in June 2017, Theuma said Fenech rang him that night. “He sounded tipsy. He told me to go ahead with the Daphne job. I didn’t do anything, he sounded drunk.” A few days later, he gave Fenech his winnings from the bet – €300,000, minus a commission. Nothing more was said about Caruana Galizia. But a few days later, Fenech summoned him and gave him an envelope stuffed with cash. “I asked him, ‘What’s this?’ He said: ‘It’s the €150,000 to have Daphne killed.’” The hitmen were given a €30,000 deposit and began scoping the journalist’s movements. Theuma was given a burner phone to contact them with. The witness said he took the phone with him to Disneyland for a family holiday, and that Fenech wanted reassurance he had not left Malta without it. The businessman became impatient as time passed. “Yorgen would ask me every few days: ‘When will they kill her?’ Once, he was on his boat and texted me to say he was preparing champagne in case it happened.” Theuma said Fenech helped to plot Caruana Galizia’s routine, identifying a cafe and restaurant that she frequented. The witness broke down as he described the moment he learned of the death from the television news. Wiping his eyes, he said: “I was living a normal life, I didn’t want for anything. Then I turned on the TV and saw that Daphne was dead. My life ended. When she was killed, my life was blown up.” He also revealed he had been in regular contact by text message with Caruana Galizia’s sons, Matthew and Paul. He said: “I was involved in their mother’s murder, and they speak to me. They tell me I will feel better after the trial. But I know I won’t. The remorse is too great.” Fenech, who is on trial for complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, denies the charges. The trial continues.

title: Mike Lindell faces legal complaint over pillow giveaway amid run for Minnesota governor
summary: Judge finds probable cause to believe the MyPillow founder violated campaign law by handing out free pillows at event
body: An administrative law judge in Minnesota has found probable cause to believe Mike Lindell, candidate for Minnesota governor and the MyPillow founder, violated campaign finance law by handing out free pillows at a public event last month. In a four-page ruling issued on Thursday, Judge Nicholas Lienesch found that a complaint against Lindell had enough to move on to an evidentiary hearing in front of a three-judge administrative panel. “There is probable cause to believe that the pillows in this case were a thing of monetary value and were not explicitly exempted by any provision of the statute,” Lienesch wrote. “There is probable cause to believe that the pillows were distributed in order to induce a voter to vote in a particular way at an election.” Lindell, one of Donald Trump’s most reliable political allies and a US pillow advertising fixture, is running for Minnesota governor against six Republican rivals, including Minnesota’s house speaker, Lisa Demuth, and state GOP-endorsed candidate Kendall Qualls, and seven Democrats, including the Minnesota senator Amy Klobuchar. The candidates face a primary election next week to tease out who will go head-to-head in November. Reached for comment on Friday, Lindell argued the pillow giveaway complaint was “complete nonsense”. “It’s been a nonstop campaign since President Trump endorsed me three weeks ago,” he said, claiming that he had checked out the pillow giveaway ahead of time with Minnesota’s campaign finance board. “We got everything completely OKed. This a just a catch-up right before the primary to put doubt in people’s heads. We did everything right. There was no law broken, period. “It’s just an attack,”Lindell added. “It’s disgusting.” On Tuesday, Lindell said he was stepping down as MyPillow CEO to focus his “time and energy” on his run for governor, calling it “one of the biggest decisions” of his life. The complaint against Lindell was brought by Dan Fiskum, a Democrat running for state senate, saying that Lindell threw free pillows from the company he started at an event at a Fourth of July parade in Delano, Minnesota. Under Minnesota law, it is impermissible to give away or promise something of monetary value to induce a voter to vote in a particular way or refrain from voting. Food and beverages valued at less than $5 are exempted. Lindell has said that the pillows he threw were bought wholesale for $4.90 each. Thursday’s ruling does not say Lindell broke the law with the pillow distribution, but Lienesch wrote that he was determining whether “sufficient facts exist in the record to believe that a violation of the law has occurred”. Lindell’s MyPillow fortune, once valued at $300m, has diminished in recent years and he has faced defamation lawsuits and financial judgments over his claims that the 2020 US presidential election was rigged. The candidate said at a hearing on Monday that he could not see a difference between the pillows, which came with campaign literature, and typical campaign trinkets like buttons and keychains. Lindell compared the pillow giveaway to his campaign purchasing his memoir – titled What Are the Odds? From Crack Addict to CEO – and handing it out free at campaign events. The Minnesota Star Tribune reported that he was asked what the pillow was worth to people who got one. Lindell responded that most of the pillows went to kids and “those little kids, they like a good night’s sleep and hug that pillow”, but acknowledged that sleep patterns “would be subjective between each individual”. For the adults who received a pillow, Lindell said: “The gift of sleep, I don’t know, it’s all subjective. I don’t think any one of them said: ‘Oh I’m getting a value of $10 and I’m getting it for free.’”

title: Messy is chic again. But is the world ready for my kind of crumpled grubbiness?
summary: All my clothes are stained and creased and my house is cluttered, so I should be thrilled by this moment. But it’s naive to think we are about to be tolerant of the real mess of life, writes Emma Beddington
body: Stand down Stacey Solomon; hush, quiet luxury: mess is back, though in this household, and I suspect many others, it never went away. “Messiness in all its aesthetic glory is being celebrated in a meaningful way,” Susie Lau writes in this month’s Elle, highlighting some recent fashion mess – dirty shirt cuffs and frayed embroidery at Prada; battered handbags at Chanel; an “extreme-treated denim” homage to the walk of shame at Diesel. Beauty and homes are on a similar trajectory, apparently, with morning-after makeup and interiors that make a virtue of clutter and imperfection, “from unmade beds to breakfast leftovers”. The mess revival Lau observes in style has also been gathering momentum in other areas: goblin mode, bed rotting and sloppy, blurred Instagram photo dumps. Now “gen Z is drinking again” (74% of them, up from 66% in 2023 according to a drinks industry study), there seems to be a broader sobriety backlash brewing and cigarettes are, depressingly, back in fashion (deployed as accessories by Kylie Jenner, Dua Lipa, Hailey Bieber and many more). All my clothes are stained and crumpled and the clutter in my house is so over the top I think it might be load-bearing: I should be thrilled by this moment. I’m certainly delighted that, as Lau observes, resistance to the smooth-edged, uncanny aesthetics of AI tasteslop and cleaner-than-thou self-optimisation is ramping up. Please don’t tell me about your microbiome – it’s so annoying it’s messing up my parasympathetic nervous system. But instead, I find myself thinking there’s mess and mess, and the boring kind is never cool. Because while the aesthetics of mess, the performance of it, have become acceptable, even aspirational, I don’t think we’re any more tolerant of the real mess of life. Sexy dishevelment, visual signifiers of a wild night, an online breadcrumb trail of exciting unravelling, a curated tablescape of mismatched crockery, spills and stubbed-out cigs – chic. But being broke, hurting, feeling unable to cope, being too unwell or unhappy to do the dishes, or to wash? Still decidedly unchic. It’s something Kathryn Jezer-Morton pointed out in the Cut recently, in a piece on how struggling is the last social media taboo. “There are few if any accessible scripts for our ambivalent feelings and our everyday confusion,” Jezer-Morton writes, noting how breakups, illness, money troubles and other properly painful stuff tends only to be aired online after the event, or handled with polished, almost-corporate restraint, finessed into upbeat narratives of progress and personal growth (or, I would add, metabolised into glib, palatably fun content). Jezer-Morton sees this partly as a byproduct of personal brand building (especially as a wobbly economy makes presenting a polished version of yourself feel like a fiscal imperative). It’s also about how social media spaces don’t feel safe. Showing the pale underbelly of your real mess is exposing, and who wants Meta and the rest of the tech bros data harvesting their vulnerability? In the fragmented wild west of TikTok and obscurer corners of Substack, there are pockets of rawer realness – people struggling day-to-day with chronic illness, poor mental health or lack of money, without a neat redemption arc – but most of the current mess renaissance feels about as authentic as intentionally distressed denim. It’s probably naive to imagine showing genuine mess – literal or figurative – online is even an option, but I’m a veteran of the early internet, when we did exactly that, probably unwisely. Now I’ve retreated, like everyone else, into posting bland pictures of pets and plants rather than the used interdental brushes and unpaid bills on my desk. Uncomfortable feelings get elliptical vague-posts at most; more often silence. Because life is messy in repetitive, unglamorous ways that don’t make us look good. Can that ever be cool? Stranger things have happened. After all, fashion can make anything desirable: a DHL uniform T-shirt for £185; experimental Japanese garments that make the wearer look like a Louise Bourgeois spider trapped in a bin bag. But I suppose the danger is that if tastemakers made grubby, humdrum, untidy lives cool, they’d soon have to make them uncool again. I’d love ordinary mess to become timelessly chic, like a crisp white shirt, but I fear that’s about as likely as me keeping one clean. • Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Kemi Badenoch’s weird week: defence of ex-neo-Nazi raises questions over Tory direction
summary: Some in party are delighted by leader’s tack rightwards but opponents have savoured latest Conservative controversy
body: There was a moment in the middle of this week when a news alert raised eyebrows among the politically committed. It read: “Kemi Badenoch: Former neo-Nazi candidate would just be sorting out bins.” It was a collection of words that might prompt palpitations in the most sanguine of communications professionals, followed by panicked advice that retreat was necessary. But as a deeply weird week for the Conservative party came to a close on Friday, its leader appeared adamant she would hold the line. With Badenoch accused of aping Reform UK on policy and purging centrists from her party in recent weeks, her decision to stand by a man who was jailed after creating sexualised images of a Jewish MP and calling her a “rodent” has prompted concerns about the leader of the opposition’s political antennae and the Tories’ wider strategy. On Monday it emerged that Joshua Bonehill-Paine, a former neo-Nazi activist convicted of the sexist and antisemitic harassment of the Labour peer Luciana Berger, had been selected as a Conservative candidate for a local election in Somerset. A little over 48 hours later, Bonehill-Paine – creator of pro-right viral AI clips that often depict politicians on the left in an ugly light – withdrew his candidacy, saying Badenoch had instead asked him to become an adviser to the party’s culture and integration commission, focusing on how young men become radicalised. As pressure mounted, Badenoch said she was “sad” that Bonehill-Paine felt he “won’t be given the space to explain his position and represent his community”, chastising those who had called her judgment into question. “Piling on [people who have changed] and trying to get them cancelled may be sport for other parties,” she wrote on social media. “But this is a different Conservative party.” Her stance has left some in her party delighted by her persistent pugilism but others scratching their heads and looking to the door. For opponents, it has been a moment to savour, with Reform saying her support “beggars belief”, while locally focused Liberal Democrats delighted in criticising Badenoch’s insistence that as a councillor Bonehill-Paine would only have been “looking at parking, sorting out bins”. The embrace of Bonehill-Paine has come at a critical moment in Badenoch’s leadership. Last month she embarked on a purge of the Conservative parliamentary party, writing in the Telegraph that it was “not a retirement home for failed politicians” and warning that anyone who supported net zero targets or Britain’s membership of the European convention on human rights (ECHR) would be blocked from standing as a candidate in the next election. The former minister Gavin Barwell lost the whip, and another former cabinet member, Grant Shapps, was blocked from standing again for the party. Sources said multiple Reform members had been blocked from joining the party. “To do that while welcoming this chap has definitely raised a few eyebrows,” one source said. The purge had left many young Tories and centrists politically homeless, said the former Tory activist Cody Butler, who resigned last weekend as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network and left the party. He said centrists, members worried about the climate crisis and conservation, and remainers – those who Margaret Thatcher may have referred to as “Wets” – were “running out of road”. “We keep hearing the parliamentary party has never been more united,” Butler said. “But I think the real truth is the arsonists have taken control, and they’re trying to set the great oak tree of Toryism alight.” Badenoch also announced this week that a Conservative government would evict foreign nationals with leave to remain from social housing, prompting Reform’s Zia Yusuf to accuse her of trying to copy his party’s policy, and the homelessness charity Shelter to warn the policy would “drive up homelessness and put extreme pressure on councils”. Despite the private worries of some in the Tory party, delight in Badenoch’s unabashed tack rightwards is not difficult to find among the rank and file. “It’s going down really well,” said one MP. “The party thinks Kemi is doing brilliantly.” A senior Conservative adviser said the party was being clear on what it believed and why. “At the last election, voters would tell us they didn’t know what the party stood for. Kemi is changing that,” they said. But rightwingers are not the only ones enjoying the ride. Labour sources said they had been looking on and reaching for the popcorn this week. “Just as you think Kemi might finally be sorting out their tent, she spends a week focused on totally irrelevant nonsense,” said one. “Nothing trumps a person’s instincts and hers are just wrong.” In the yellow corner, gleeful Lib Dems point out that under Badenoch the Tories seem to be showing little interest in taking back any of the 60 seats they lost directly to their party in 2024 as part of a drubbing in which the Conservatives shed a record 251 seats. Once the near unchallenged flagbearer of middle England, the Conservatives now have zero MPs in Oxfordshire, for the first time since 1777. A committed leftwing hiker could walk from Land’s End to London without passing through a Tory constituency. Despite Badenoch’s insistence that the May local elections showed “the Conservatives are coming back”, the party lost about 500 councillors in England and ceded control of three local authorities. Even now, the Tories are skittering along at 19% of the vote, compared with Reform on 24 and Labour on 23, according to Politico’s poll of polls. A senior Lib Dem source said: “It was widely expected that the Conservatives were at their lowest ebb in 2024 and would quickly start making progress. In fact, it’s us that have taken loads off them rather than the other way round. “Whether it is [on] fighting for more action on the climate or defending human rights, the Conservatives sound more like Nigel Farage than former leaders who were popular with middle England. It is genuinely giving us the biggest opportunity against them we have ever had.” Given current polling – and the results of the 2024 election in which the Conservatives lost about a third of their votes to Reform – attempting to woo those who voted for Farage was logical, said the pollster John Curtice. “The Tories are in a pretty dire state but not quite as dire as they were a few months ago,” he said. “By my calculation, they are now losing around 17% of those votes to Farage.” Polling indicates Badenoch’s personal approval rating is on the up: a YouGov poll last month put her net favourability at -11, the highest of any Conservative leader in more than five years. Curtice said the Tories were facing a dilemma: whether to try to build a more centrist coalition with the voters who had stuck with the party, or try to win back Reform voters. “But in [Reform] voters’ minds they are the party who failed to deliver Brexit properly and who created the Boris wave,” he said. “And the more fundamental problem is not to do with ideology, it’s to do with competence. Partygate trashed their ethical reputation, and [Liz] Truss trashed their reputation on the economy.” Robert Hayward, a Conservative peer and polling analyst, played down the theory that Badenoch was increasingly moving the Conservatives to the right but said she would have to adapt against a Labour party under Andy Burnham. Asked where it currently looked as if the Conservatives would gain seats on their current trajectory, Hayward was candid. “I don’t think that is very clear as yet, and that’s a major challenge to the party,” he said. “But it’s a problem for everyone. People’s allegiance to any political party is weaker now than at any moment during my lifetime. Who knows where we’ll be in December 2026, never mind on the eve of a general election.”

title: US economy lost 23,000 jobs in July in surprise blow to Trump – as it happened
summary: Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news, as US job report dramatically misses expectations
body: Time to wrap up… US employers unexpectedly lost 23,000 jobs in July and gains for the previous two months were revised down sharply by a combined 103,000 jobs, painting a weaker picture of the labor market than past data indicated. The unemployment rate, however, held steady at 4.1%. Economists had projected an unchanged unemployment rate and 83,000 new jobs for the month. The latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics illustrates the continued summer slump in job growth amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Pressure has been mounting within the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to combat persistently high inflation, but July’s job report and its latest revisions may cool those expectations at the central bank’s next meeting. July’s job losses were concentrated in local government education, with 50,000 jobs lost, and retail, which lost 19,000. The private sector, however, gained 30,000 jobs, with growth focused once again in healthcare. Shares rose on Wall Street after the report was released, as traders calculated that the US Federal Reserve was less likely to raise interest rates in September. This also knocked the dollar. Elsewhere… Global food prices have hit their highest level in three and a half years, as summer heatwaves and conflict in Ukraine and the Middle East push up crop costs. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) index of food commodity prices rose last month to its highest level since January 2023, after a jump in prices for cereals, sugar and vegetable oil. The US aviation regulator has ordered inspections of the fuselages of Boeing 737 Max planes for possible cracks in a component. The Federal Aviation Administration airworthiness directive will affect an estimated 471 aircraft and follows reports of cracks in earlier Boeing models. The inspections, which will start from September, follow a similar FAA regime for previous Boeing 737 Next Generation models dating back to 2021. UK house prices were broadly stagnant in July as prospective buyers were squeezed by higher mortgage rates, uncertainty around the Middle East and stretched affordability, according to the lender Lloyds. Have a lovely weekend! GW Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management, argues that today’s jobs report is a “game changer”, because it takes some of the focus off fears of high US inflation. Zaccarelli adds, via CNBC: “Before today, many were expecting that the Fed had no choice but to raise rates in order to fight stubbornly high inflation, because the job market was so strong, but this report shows that isn’t the case.” Gold has hit a ⁠seven week high after today’s unexpected drop in US payrolls. Spot gold jumped by 3%, and is now trading around $4,345 an ounce. July’s weak US jobs report underlines there is no need for the Federal Reserve to rush into an interest rate rise, argues Steve Blitz, chief US economist at TS Lombard. Say goodbye to September, maybe even December too. [Fed chair Kevin] Warsh’s reaction function is growth (it’s that simple), rooted in the strong belief that growth can be accompanied by low inflation. Inflation is a lagging indicator, and high oil prices and tariffs are working their way out of the inflation data. Given that, and strong Q2 productivity data (a residual, but Warsh will run with it in any event), there is zero chance of a rate hike. I have been writing this from the get-go from a policy bias standpoint. The softer employment data bring into question whether even a rate hike is required. Because data trends matter most, let’s wait and see how the trends work out. Point is – there is no rush for action. US wage growth also slowed last month, today’s jobs report shows. On an annual basis, wage growth eased to 3.2%, down from 3.5% in June, which is another indication that the labor market is cooling. Fawad Razaqzada, market analyst at Forex.com, says: The softer wage figures will provide some reassurance to policymakers concerned about persistent inflationary pressures, while also adding to evidence that labour demand is gradually losing steam. Today’s surprisingly weak US jobs report has cheered investors on Wall Street. That’s not because they get a kick out of other people losing their jobs, but because a weak labor market means it will be harder for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. The S&P 500 share index rose by 25.2 points, or 0.33%, at the open to 7735.18 points. The tech-focused Nasdaq saw a larger bounce – it’s up 0.7%. The US private sector did add jobs in July, points out consultancy Capital Economics: The underlying picture in the private sector was somewhat better, but still far from strong. Private payrolls grew by 30,000, led by pockets of strength in construction (+22,000) and healthcare and social assistance (22,600), although employment growth in the latter continued to slow relative to its average. These gains were partially offset by sizeable declines in retail trade (-19,400), nondurable goods manufacturing (-13,000) and financial activities (-14,000). The start of school holidays is probably responsibly for the 50,000 drop in employment in local government education last month. And bars and restaurants may have cut back on jobs as the FIFA World Cup reached its conclusion. Carson Group’s chief macro strategist Sonu Varghese explains: “Headline payrolls were really disappointing, with 23,000 jobs lost in July. But the weakness was concentrated in local government, largely due to school-calendar seasonal effects, and leisure and hospitality as the World Cup boost rolled off. The bigger picture is that unemployment fell to 4.1%, its lowest in a year. Combined with low initial jobless claims, that suggests the labor market remains in solid shape despite the volatility in payrolls.” Could AI be to blame for the drop in US employment last month? Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, suggests the rise of AI bots could be a factor, saying: The interesting dynamic is the drop in the jobless rate. Another function of falling participation and the fact that data comes from a different survey. At a higher level, there could be the fingerprints of AI in this jobs report too: employers possibly replacing workers with bots. We will have to dig into the details and wait for future data to get a clearer picture of that though. Nic Puckrin, a former Goldman Sachs analyst, says: On top of this, consumer confidence has crumbled and AI is swallowing thousands of white-collar jobs. So, when you look under the hood, the US economy is looking far more anaemic than the numbers suggest. Ordinary Americans are in a tough spot, while the Federal Reserve must decide whether to sacrifice employment to control inflation or vice versa.” According to outplacement firm Challenger, Grey & Christmas, AI has been the top reason given for layoffs in the last five months. The US labor force participation rate, which measures how many people are either in work or looking for a jobs, has dropped. The labor force participation rate slipped to 61.4%, which explains how the unemployment rate could fall even though the number of jobs also declined. The dollar is falling too. The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against a basket of other currencies, is down 0.4% today. That’s lifted the pound up by half a cent to $1.35. Such a bad jobs report is sending ripples through the financial markets. Traders are rushing to slash bets on a rise in US interest rates next month, concluding that the Federal Reserve won’t want to tighten policy when the economy is shedding jobs. The rate futures market has now priced in just a 43.9% chance of Fed tightening in September, compared with 57% before the jobs report, Reuters flags. The latest Household Survey Data, just released, also shows what’s going on in the US labor market. Here’s a flavour: Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rates for teenagers (12.1 percent) and people who are Hispanic (4.6 percent) declined in July. The jobless rates for adult men (3.9 percent), adult women (3.7 percent), and people who are White (3.6 percent), Black (6.3 percent), or Asian (4.0 percent) showed little or no change over the month. Among the unemployed, the number of people on temporary layoff increased by 153,000 to 921,000 in July. The number of permanent job losers changed little at 1.7 million. In July, the number of people jobless less than 5 weeks edged down to 2.0 million and is down by 344,000 over the year. The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more) edged down over the month to 1.8 million but changed little over the year. The long-term unemployed accounted for 25.5 percent of all unemployed people in July. Here’s the details of where jobs were lost across the US economy last month. Employment in local government education declined by 50,000 in July. Retail trade lost 19,000 jobs in July, including a 21,000 drop at warehouse clubs, supercenters, and other general merchandise retailers and a 5,000 drop in employment at gasoline stations and fuel dealers. Employment in financial activities fell by 14,000. But….employment in health care continued its upward trend, rising by 22,000 Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; construction; manufacturing; wholesale trade; transportation and warehousing; information; professional and business services; social assistance; leisure and hospitality; and other services. Not only did the US economy lose jobs in July, it created fewer jobs than first thought in May and June. The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for May has been revised down by 66,000, from +129,000 to +63,000, and the change for June was revised down by 37,000, from +57,000 to +20,000. Newsflash: The US economy shed jobs last month. The US nonfarm payroll shows a fall of 23,000 jobs in July, startling economists who had expected…

title: Trump’s attorney general pick Todd Blanche appears to clear last hurdle for confirmation
summary: Bill Cassidy, Republican seen as a decisive holdout, said he is prepared to back Trump’s former personal lawyer
body: Bill Cassidy, the US Republican senator seen as the decisive holdout on Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general, announced on Friday that he will support the pick, setting the stage for a major win for Donald Trump. Confirmation that Cassidy, of Louisiana, is prepared to back Blanche – Trump’s former personal lawyer, and a loyal ally of the president – appeared to clear the last hurdle of his confirmation process, which had been challenged by the defections of the Republican senators Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins. Blanche is already serving as acting attorney general. “I will vote for Mr Blanche,” Cassidy said in a US Senate floor speech on Friday morning. “Mr Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this, but the choice is not between perfection and Mr Blanche; it is between Mr Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump, and who indeed may not be as good as Mr Blanche.” With Cassidy now on board, Blanche is expected to be confirmed by a narrow margin, probably along party lines, as the Senate works through a final vote series before senators leave for the five-week August recess that starts this weekend. Cassidy, who lost his Louisiana primary in May after facing two challengers, including one backed by Trump, had faced weeks of pressure from the White House and had voiced concerns about “lawfare” at the justice department before announcing his decision. Murkowski, Alaska’s moderate Republican senator, had announced earlier on Friday that she would not vote for Blanche’s confirmation, leaving his path to the job down to a single Republican vote. Murkowski’s announcement came a day after Trump, speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday, was asked about his fraying relationships with Republican critics including Murkowski and Cassidy and whether the president would reach out to either Republican senator to save the vote. “I’ll reach out to whoever I have to, but anybody voting against [Blanche] would be doing a great disservice to the country,” Trump told reporters. “People have such unbelievable respect” for Blanche, he claimed, expressing hope that reaching out to those lawmakers “won’t be necessary”. Maine’s Susan Collins had already said she will oppose Blanche’s confirmation over concerns about the independence of the US Department of Justice, and with Murkowski’s opposition now confirmed, Cassidy had been the last undecided Republican vote standing between Blanche and confirmation. Murkowski and Cassidy were among the handful of Republicans who voted to convict Trump after his 2021 impeachment over the January 6 Capitol riot. After the Oval Office meeting, Trump acknowledged the political toll his feuds with GOP holdouts have taken. “Look, I don’t regret it. You do what you have to do,” Trump told Punchbowl News. “And just so you understand, they voted to impeach me … In all fairness, you think that I’m going to support somebody that voted to impeach me?” She took her stance even though Blanche confirmed in writing the controversial fund was dead. Experts say Trump could easily reverse it. Murkowski said the Senate only currently has leverage over the fund because Blanche’s nomination to head the Department of Justice is pending necessary confirmation by the upper congressional chamber. Blanche had persuaded the Senate judiciary committee in a 12-10 vote in his favor earlier this week only because he promised Republican holdouts that he would not pursue the payout fund. Blanche issued a formal order late on Sunday terminating Trump’s $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” slush fund designed to compensate political allies who had been “targeted” by the justice department, including prosecutions of January 6 insurrectionists. That move followed weeks of negotiations with two Republican senators who were blocking his nomination to become attorney general – Thom Tillis and John Cornyn, who were eventually swayed by Blanche. Murkowski posted on X on Friday, praising Blanche but then saying “ultimately” she would oppose his nomination, a position she took on Tuesday and is now sticking with. “The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration. I hope Mr Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case,” she wrote, as part of a much longer post on the topic. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, but Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, who was just released from the hospital, is not attending sessions because of his health.
